title: Type 2 Diabetes: Confirm the Diagnosis, Classify Risk, Start the Right Plan
bottomLine: Type 2 diabetes diagnosis uses validated Canadian laboratory criteria and confirmation when the patient is asymptomatic. Initial management is not A1C-only: classify the diabetes phenotype, assess cardiorenal risk and complications, address health-behaviour/support needs, and select pharmacotherapy that fits glycemic goals, cardiovascular/kidney disease, hypoglycemia risk, weight goals, access and preference.
recognize: Polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, recurrent infection or weight change can occur, but many people are asymptomatic at diagnosis.
Marked weight loss, ketosis, autoimmune history or rapid metabolic deterioration should prompt reconsideration of routine type-2 classification.
differentiate: A1C can be misleading when red-cell turnover, hemoglobinopathy, severe anemia, advanced renal/hepatic disease or other conditions affect accuracy.
Symptomatic severe hyperglycemia/ketosis is an acute management problem and should not wait for routine outpatient confirmatory testing.
assessment: Assess symptoms, weight trajectory, pregnancy status, medications such as glucocorticoids/antipsychotics, family history and features of insulin deficiency.
At diagnosis assess BP, lipids/ASCVD, renal function/albuminuria, smoking, neuropathy/foot risk and medication/nutrition access.
workup: Use fasting plasma glucose, A1C and/or OGTT/random glucose criteria appropriately and confirm an isolated diagnostic-range result when asymptomatic.
Use ketones/electrolytes/acid-base testing urgently when metabolic decompensation is possible.
management: Integrate nutrition/activity/self-management education and weight management from diagnosis.

When pharmacotherapy is indicated, metformin remains an initial option for many adults, while cardiorenal indications can justify SGLT2-inhibitor and/or GLP-1 receptor-agonist therapy independent of A1C alone.
Use insulin promptly for marked symptomatic hyperglycemia or metabolic decompensation.
medicationSafety: Match drug choice to eGFR, HF/CKD/ASCVD, pregnancy, hypoglycemia risk, weight, adverse effects, cost and interactions.
redFlags: Severe dehydration or altered mental status
Vomiting/abdominal pain on an SGLT2 inhibitor
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and explain that treatment decisions include heart/kidney protection as well as glucose.
followUp: Reassess glycemia, medication tolerance, complications/risk factors and access after treatment initiation or change.
examTrap: Treating A1C as the only treatment target or delaying acute insulin/urgent care because an outpatient confirmatory test is still pending.
oneLinePearl: Diagnose correctly, classify the phenotype, then treat glucose and cardiorenal risk together.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Clinical Practice Guidelines — diagnosis/classification
Diabetes Canada 2024 Pharmacologic Glycemic Management of Type 2 Diabetes

title: Type 1 Diabetes: Basal Insulin Is Physiologic Replacement, Not an Optional Meal Drug
bottomLine: Type 1 diabetes is absolute insulin deficiency. Build an individualized basal-bolus or pump regimen that covers basal needs and food/correction requirements, and never omit basal insulin simply because the patient is fasting or ill; dose may need adjustment, but insulin interruption can precipitate DKA rapidly.
recognize: Pump interruption creates rapid insulin deficiency because no long-acting depot exists.
Exercise, illness, alcohol, menstrual/pregnancy changes and renal function can materially alter insulin needs.
differentiate: Basal insulin covers background hepatic glucose output; prandial insulin covers carbohydrate/meal exposure; correction insulin addresses above-target glucose.
Holding prandial insulin for no meal is different from withholding all insulin in type 1 diabetes.
assessment: Review CGM/SMBG patterns, meal timing/carbohydrate strategy, hypoglycemia, ketones, exercise, injection/pump sites and psychosocial treatment burden.
Assess pregnancy plans and access to insulin/supplies/glucagon/ketone testing.
workup: Use A1C plus CGM/SMBG patterns to evaluate chronic control and ketone testing during illness/hyperglycemia according to the sick-day plan.
Investigate unexplained recurrent hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia for regimen, device, absorption and comorbidity causes.
management: Use individualized basal-bolus injections or pump therapy with education on carbohydrate/meal dosing, correction and exercise/illness adjustments.
Ensure glucagon access and a backup plan for pump failure or interrupted supplies.
medicationSafety: Never abruptly stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes without a clinician-directed replacement strategy.
Insulin concentration/device errors can cause severe hypo- or hyperglycemia; verify product, device and units carefully.
counselling: Teach sick-day rules, ketone testing, driving/exercise hypoglycemia prevention and glucagon use.
followUp: Use diabetes-team support and review time-below/above-range, severe events and treatment burden—not A1C alone.
examTrap: Holding all insulin because a person with type 1 diabetes is NPO.
oneLinePearl: No meal may change prandial insulin; it does not remove the physiologic need for basal insulin.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Glycemic Management in Adults with Type 1 Diabetes

title: Diabetes Medications Beyond Metformin: Choose for Cardiorenal Benefit, Hypoglycemia, Weight, and Access
bottomLine: After—or sometimes alongside—metformin, choose glucose-lowering therapy from the patient's cardiorenal disease, A1C distance from goal, hypoglycemia risk, weight goals, renal function, adverse effects, cost/access and preference. The strongest cardiorenal indication can matter even when A1C is already at target.
recognize: SGLT2 inhibitors and selected GLP-1 receptor agonists can provide cardiovascular/renal benefit beyond glucose lowering in appropriate patients.
Sulfonylureas and insulin have greater hypoglycemia risk; frailty, CKD and inconsistent intake increase that risk.
differentiate: A drug's A1C-lowering potency is not the same as its cardiorenal outcome value.
DPP-4 inhibitor plus GLP-1 receptor agonist is generally not a useful combination because mechanisms overlap without added outcome benefit.
assessment: Assess ASCVD/high CV risk, HF, CKD/albuminuria, eGFR, weight goals, hypoglycemia history, GI tolerance, cost/coverage and injection preference.
workup: Use A1C and glucose monitoring appropriate to the regimen; monitor renal function and class-specific parameters where treatment decisions depend on them.
management: Select/add therapy from current Diabetes Canada 2024 pharmacotherapy guidance and individualized priorities.
Use insulin when severe symptomatic hyperglycemia or metabolic decompensation makes gradual oral/injectable escalation unsafe.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause genital infection, volume depletion and euglycemic DKA; use sick-day/perioperative holding guidance.
GLP-1 receptor agonists can cause substantial GI effects and require pancreatobiliary/gastroparesis context.
Sulfonylureas require hypoglycemia caution, especially in CKD/frailty.
counselling: Explain why a drug may be chosen for kidney/heart protection even when glucose looks controlled.
followUp: Reassess glycemia, weight, hypoglycemia, renal function, tolerance and access after changes; intensify or de-intensify rather than accumulating ineffective drugs.
examTrap: Rejecting an SGLT2 inhibitor/GLP-1RA solely because A1C is already at target despite a compelling cardiorenal indication.
oneLinePearl: Beyond metformin, choose the drug for the patient—not only for the A1C.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada 2024 Pharmacologic Glycemic Management of Type 2 Diabetes

title: Insulin Initiation and Titration: Match the Pattern Before Adding More Insulin
bottomLine: Insulin titration is pattern-based. Basal insulin primarily targets fasting/background hyperglycemia; prandial insulin targets meal-related excursions. If fasting glucose is controlled but A1C remains high, adding more basal insulin can cause overnight hypoglycemia without fixing postprandial exposure.
recognize: Persistent fasting hyperglycemia can support basal adjustment when adherence, technique, illness and nocturnal hypoglycemia have been considered.
A large bedtime-to-morning drop or recurrent overnight lows suggests excessive basal insulin rather than a need for further titration.
differentiate: Basal, prandial and correction insulin have different physiologic roles.
Severe symptomatic hyperglycemia/ketosis needs urgent treatment rather than slow outpatient titration.
assessment: Review glucose/CGM patterns, timing/doses, meal consistency, injection technique/sites, hypoglycemia, renal function, activity and missed doses.
Confirm insulin product/concentration/device to avoid medication errors.
workup: Use fasting/premeal/postmeal/CGM patterns to identify which part of the regimen is failing rather than titrating from A1C alone.
Investigate recurrent unexplained hypoglycemia or high insulin requirement for renal, endocrine, infection or adherence/device causes.
management: Start and titrate basal insulin using a validated patient/clinic algorithm and individualized fasting target; add prandial strategy when postmeal hyperglycemia remains despite appropriate basal control.
Simplify/de-intensify in frailty or recurrent hypoglycemia when treatment burden exceeds benefit.
medicationSafety: Over-basalization causes nocturnal/fasting hypoglycemia and weight gain without correcting meal excursions.
Do not use one universal dose algorithm across type 1 diabetes, pregnancy, frailty and acute illness.
counselling: Teach product/device identification, injection technique, hypoglycemia treatment and how titration decisions use patterns rather than isolated readings.
followUp: Review glucose patterns soon after initiation/change and adjust one physiologic problem at a time.
examTrap: Increasing basal insulin because A1C is high even though fasting glucose is already controlled and overnight lows are occurring.
oneLinePearl: Fix fasting glucose with basal; fix meal excursions with prandial strategy—do not ask basal insulin to do both jobs.

title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring: Read Patterns, Time in Range, and Safety—Not One Sensor Point
bottomLine: CGM is most useful as a pattern tool. Interpret time below/in/above range, overnight and postmeal trends, variability, treatment timing and data sufficiency; a single interstitial sensor value can lag blood glucose during rapid change and should be confirmed when symptoms or the clinical decision do not fit the sensor.
recognize: Recurrent overnight lows, postmeal spikes or large variability often identify a regimen problem that A1C hides.
Time below range is a safety outcome and may justify de-intensification even when A1C appears excellent.
differentiate: Interstitial glucose can lag capillary glucose during rapid rise/fall.
Compression lows, sensor failure and medication/interference issues can create misleading readings depending on device.
assessment: Review data completeness, sensor use, meal/activity/insulin timing, hypoglycemia awareness and whether symptoms match the trace.
Assess alarm burden, cost/access and ability to act safely on alerts.
workup: Use standardized ambulatory glucose profile/time-range metrics when sufficient data exist.
Confirm with capillary/laboratory glucose when symptoms, severe low/high alarms or treatment decisions are discordant with CGM.
management: Adjust basal, meal/correction therapy, timing and behaviour from recurring patterns rather than reacting to every arrow.
Use individualized targets for pregnancy, frailty and high hypoglycemia risk rather than one universal range goal.
medicationSafety: Avoid insulin stacking from repeated reaction to CGM arrows without considering insulin-on-board and lag.
Alarm settings should improve safety rather than create disabling alert fatigue.
redFlags: Sensor result inconsistent with clinical condition
counselling: Teach trend arrows, sensor lag, confirmation rules, alarms and when ketone testing is needed.
followUp: Review CGM after meaningful regimen changes and focus on recurrent patterns, severe events and treatment burden.
examTrap: Giving repeated correction insulin for a rapidly changing CGM value without considering sensor lag or insulin-on-board.
oneLinePearl: CGM is a movie, not a photograph—treat the pattern, not one pixel.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Monitoring Glycemic Control guidance
Diabetes Canada blood glucose monitoring update

title: DKA: Fluids, Potassium, Insulin, Dextrose, and the Precipitating Cause
bottomLine: DKA is a ketone/acidosis emergency, not merely a high-glucose emergency. Restore volume, evaluate potassium before/during insulin, continue insulin long enough to clear ketosis/acidosis using dextrose when needed, monitor electrolytes frequently, and find the precipitating cause; SGLT2-associated DKA can occur with only modest glucose elevation.
recognize: Vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, tachypnea/Kussmaul breathing and altered mental status are concerning.
Common triggers include infection, interrupted insulin/pump failure, new diabetes, MI/stroke and medications including SGLT2 inhibitors.
differentiate: Starvation/alcoholic ketosis and lactic acidosis can mimic parts of DKA.
Urine ketones may underrepresent beta-hydroxybutyrate-predominant DKA; blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is preferable where available.
assessment: Assess ABCs, perfusion, volume, mental status, infection/ischemia, pregnancy and medication history including SGLT2 inhibitor use.
Obtain ECG when significant potassium disturbance is possible.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, bicarbonate/pH, beta-hydroxybutyrate/ketones and anion-gap assessment plus precipitant-directed testing.
Do not use glucose normalization alone as the endpoint of DKA resolution.
management: Use a validated hospital DKA protocol with isotonic fluid, potassium-guided insulin, dextrose when glucose falls before ketoacidosis resolves, and frequent biochemical reassessment.
medicationSafety: Insulin can dangerously worsen severe hypokalemia; potassium status must guide therapy.
SGLT2-associated DKA can be euglycemic and requires drug discontinuation/acute management.
counselling: After recovery teach sick-day insulin continuity, ketone testing, pump-failure backup and SGLT2 sick-day/perioperative rules.
followUp: Address the precipitant, access/adherence barriers and follow-up before discharge.
examTrap: Stopping DKA therapy because glucose normalized while ketosis/anion-gap acidosis persists—or missing euglycemic DKA.
oneLinePearl: DKA ends when the ketoacidosis resolves, not when the glucose looks better.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada hyperglycemic-emergency and sick-day guidance

title: HHS: Profound Dehydration and Hyperosmolality Need Controlled Correction
bottomLine: HHS is a severe hyperglycemic/hyperosmolar dehydration syndrome with less prominent ketoacidosis than DKA. Restore volume carefully, monitor sodium/potassium/osmolality/renal function and neurologic status, add insulin after initial fluid/potassium assessment, and avoid overly rapid osmotic correction.
recognize: Older adults may present with profound dehydration, weakness, confusion, seizures or coma with extreme hyperglycemia.
Infection, missed treatment, MI/stroke and medications commonly precipitate HHS.
differentiate: DKA has prominent ketosis/acidosis and often faster onset; mixed DKA/HHS presentations occur and should be managed according to the dangerous physiology present.
Corrected sodium/tonicity and osmolality matter because glucose-driven water shifts can make the measured sodium misleading.
assessment: Assess mental status, perfusion, volume depletion, urine output, infection/ischemia, medication history and baseline frailty/comorbidity.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes, renal function, calculated/measured osmolality as appropriate, ketones/acid-base and precipitant testing.
Trend sodium/osmolality during treatment rather than treating glucose in isolation.
management: Use hospital protocol with controlled isotonic fluid resuscitation, potassium-guided insulin and electrolyte/osmolality monitoring.
Treat the precipitant and use thrombosis prevention/supportive care according to acute-care risk.
medicationSafety: Rapid osmotic shifts can cause neurologic harm; correction pace is monitored rather than improvised.
Insulin and fluids can change potassium/sodium quickly, especially with renal impairment.
counselling: After recovery review hydration, medication access, illness plans and early hyperglycemia warning signs.
followUp: Ensure precipitating illness and diabetes-regimen/access failures are resolved before discharge.
examTrap: Treating only the glucose while ignoring osmolality, sodium, neurologic status and profound volume depletion.
oneLinePearl: HHS is a dehydration/osmolality emergency with hyperglycemia—not just a glucose emergency.

title: Hypoglycemia: Treat the Low, Then Prevent the Next One
bottomLine: Hypoglycemia treatment is incomplete until the cause is identified and recurrence risk is reduced. Treat immediately according to consciousness/swallowing ability, then review insulin/secretagogues, meals, exercise, alcohol, renal function, frailty, food security and hypoglycemia awareness; recurrent lows are a medication-safety signal, not a reason to tell the patient simply to eat more.
recognize: Adrenergic symptoms include tremor, sweating, palpitations and hunger; neuroglycopenia causes confusion, visual/behaviour change, seizure or coma.
Older adults may present with falls, weakness or delirium and may have reduced warning symptoms.
differentiate: A conscious patient safe to swallow can use rapidly absorbed carbohydrate; severe inability to self-treat requires glucagon or IV glucose and emergency support.
Sulfonylurea/long-acting insulin episodes may recur after apparent initial correction.
assessment: Check glucose when feasible without delaying treatment; assess airway, consciousness, seizure/trauma.
Review doses/timing, missed meals, exercise, alcohol, renal/hepatic change, medication errors and food access.
workup: For diabetes-related episodes, analyze glucose/CGM patterns and medication exposure.
Persistent unexplained hypoglycemia without relevant therapy needs a dedicated diagnostic evaluation rather than assuming poor intake.
management: Use fast carbohydrate with repeat glucose assessment for an awake patient, and glucagon or IV glucose for severe episodes according to setting/protocol.
Reduce/reshape the causative regimen and prescribe/teach glucagon for high-risk patients/supports where appropriate.
medicationSafety: CKD, frailty and irregular intake amplify insulin/secretagogue risk.
Driving/work safety and hypoglycemia unawareness require explicit counselling and sometimes target de-intensification.
counselling: Teach fast-carbohydrate treatment, recheck, glucagon and prevention strategies; address food insecurity directly.
followUp: Any severe/recurrent episode needs prompt medication review and prevention plan, with CGM/diabetes-team support where appropriate.
examTrap: Correcting the glucose and sending the patient home without changing the medication/timing that caused the event.
oneLinePearl: Treat the glucose now; treat the cause before the next low.
